summary:
LUNAR OPS is an interactive 3D web-based mission planning and lunar landing site analysis platform built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, and a Python FastAPI scientific engine powered by NASA JPL DE421 SPICE ephemeris kernels. 

It directly addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator Challenge by transforming complex astrodynamics data into an intuitive dual-mode interface. Mission planners, educators, and the public can inspect candidate Artemis South Pole sites (such as Shackleton Rim and Malapert Massif) across a 3D selenographic globe (MOON_ME frame) or step directly onto the lunar terrain in a 360-degree First-Person Astronaut Surface POV. 

By sliding an interactive 14-day mission timeline, users visualize real-time Sun and Earth trajectories relative to the local horizon, accurately evaluating solar elevation, azimuth, incident solar power flux (W/m²), terrain slope safety, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows critical for sustainable lunar exploration.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

LUNAR OPS is a full-stack scientific mission control and 3D lunar landing site evaluation platform designed for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator Challenge. Missions to the Lunar South Pole face extreme illumination and communication constraints where a few hundred meters of elevation difference can mean the difference between near-continuous solar power and permanent darkness.

Our platform solves this by coupling a high-precision astrodynamics backend (powered by NASA JPL DE421 SPICE ephemeris kernels) with a dual-mode 3D WebGL interface:

- Orbital 3D Selenographic Globe: Displays the Moon in the standard IAU MOON_ME reference frame (R_ref = 1737.4 km) with a selenographic graticule, polar axis, real-time solar terminator, and sun/earth vector indicators. Users can select candidate Artemis III landing sites (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, Malapert Massif, de Gerlache Rim 2, Aristarchus Plateau) or click directly anywhere on the 3D lunar surface to pick custom coordinates.

- 360° First-Person Surface EVA POV: With a single click, users transition from orbital tracking directly onto the lunar surface at a 1.85m astronaut eye height next to a 3D lunar lander module. Users can walk across site-specific 3D topography (using WASD/Arrow keys), look around 360 degrees, and visually observe the exact elevation and azimuth of the Sun and Earth above the local lunar horizon.

- Interactive 14-Day Mission Timeline: A 336-hour timeline slider allows users to scrub through time or play continuous orbital motion, dynamically updating shadows, solar elevation, azimuth, incident solar flux (W/m²), and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication line-of-sight status.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

- For Mission Planners & Engineers: Provides rapid trade-space analysis comparing solar power generation potential (W/m²), local terrain slope safety (< 8° nominal criteria), and DTE communication availability across multiple landing sites and mission epochs.

- For Educators & Public Outreach: Replaces complex tabular ephemeris outputs with an intuitive, immersive tactical HUD where anyone can experience standing on the Lunar South Pole and seeing why the Sun grazes the horizon while Earth hovers in a libration zone.

3. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

- Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js (WebGL 3D rendering, custom procedural + NASA LRO texture/bump mapping, OrbitControls, Raycasting, and Topocentric First-Person EVA camera controller), and custom CSS tactical HUD styling.

- Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Skyfield (NASA JPL SPICE kernel loader), and NumPy for matrix transformations between ICRF (J2000), MOON_ME (with physical libration Euler angles), and Local Topocentric Horizon (ENU) coordinate frames.

- Scientific Data: NASA JPL DE421 (de421.bsp) Ephemeris Kernel and NASA LRO LOLA Reference Sphere Datum (1737.4 km).

4. Creativity & Engineering Factors Considered

- First-Person Topocentric Immersion: Instead of limiting the user to an external globe, we engineered a surface-level EVA simulator where sky positions of the Sun and Earth are mathematically driven by real-time topocentric azimuth and elevation angles.

- Strict Scientific Rigor: We explicitly distinguish between Elevation and Azimuth in the local horizon frame, account for topographic horizon dip at elevated polar massifs, apply inverse-square solar distance corrections to the 1361 W/m² solar constant, and incorporate lunar optical/physical libration for Earth visibility.
